items.q: A two-input perceptron has decision line crossing the $x_1$-axis at $-1$ and the $x_2$-axis at $2$ (i.e. $\frac{x_1}{-1}+\frac{x_2}{2}=1$). Which weight set $(w_0,w_1,w_2)$ realises $w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2=0$ on this line?
items.explain: The line is $2x_1 - x_2 + 2 = 0$ (check intercepts: $x_2{=}0\Rightarrow x_1{=}{-}1$; $x_1{=}0\Rightarrow x_2{=}2$), giving $(w_0,w_1,w_2)=(2,2,-1)$ up to scale. (Mitchell, Exercise 4.1.)

items.q: Per Mitchell, the **Perceptron training rule** is guaranteed to converge to a perfect classifier only when:
options: the training data is linearly separable
items.explain: The Perceptron Convergence Theorem guarantees convergence in finite steps **iff the data is linearly separable** (and η is sufficiently small). (Mitchell §4.4.2.)

items.q: How does the **delta rule** (LMS / gradient descent) differ from the perceptron training rule in Mitchell's treatment?
options: The delta rule uses the thresholded output; the perceptron rule uses the linear output
The delta rule does gradient descent on the **unthresholded linear output** and converges (asymptotically) even when data is **not** linearly separable
The delta rule only works for Boolean inputs
items.explain: The delta rule minimizes squared error on the *unthresholded* linear unit $o=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}$, so it converges toward the best-fit weights even for non-separable data — unlike the perceptron rule, which needs separability. (Mitchell §4.4.3.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 4.2 asks you to implement $A \oplus B$ (XOR). This requires:
items.explain: XOR is not linearly separable, so a single perceptron cannot represent it; a **two-layer** network of perceptrons can. (Mitchell, Exercise 4.2.)

items.q: For a sigmoid output unit $o$, the backprop error term is $\delta = (t-o)\,o(1-o)$. The factor $o(1-o)$ is:
items.explain: $\sigma'(net)=o(1-o)$ — the sigmoid's derivative — appears via the chain rule. (Mitchell §4.5.3.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 4.8 revises backprop to use $\tanh$. The needed derivative is:
items.explain: $\tanh'(x) = 1 - \tanh^2(x)$, which replaces $o(1-o)$ in the δ formulas. (Mitchell, Exercise 4.8.)

items.q: In Mitchell's backprop with a **momentum** term $\alpha$, the weight update is $\Delta w_{ji}(n) = \eta\,\delta_j x_{ji} + \alpha\,\Delta w_{ji}(n-1)$. Momentum mainly helps by:
options: carrying velocity through flat regions and damping oscillations
removing the need for a learning rate
items.explain: Adding a fraction $\alpha$ of the previous update keeps the search moving across flat plateaus and smooths oscillations in ravines. (Mitchell §4.5.2, Exercise 4.7.)

items.q: The vanishing-gradient issue with sigmoids stems from $\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$ having maximum value:
items.explain: $\sigma'$ peaks at $x=0$ with value $0.25$; products of many such factors across layers shrink toward 0.

items.q: Alpaydin (Exercise 10.4): using **two softmax outputs** for a 2-class problem is equivalent to using:
items.explain: Softmax with $K=2$ reduces algebraically to a single logistic (sigmoid) output — softmax generalises sigmoid to many classes. (Alpaydin §10.7.)

items.q: Softmax outputs $y_i = e^{a_i}/\sum_j e^{a_j}$ always satisfy:
items.explain: Softmax produces a probability distribution: non-negative values summing to 1. (Alpaydin §10.7.)

items.q: Alpaydin's **optimal separating hyperplane** is the one that:
options: passes through the most data points
maximizes the margin (distance to the nearest instances of each class)
minimizes the number of support vectors to zero
items.explain: Among all separating hyperplanes, SVM picks the one **maximizing the margin** $2/\|W\|$ — equivalently minimizing $\tfrac12\|W\|^2$. (Alpaydin §10.9.)

items.q: After solving the SVM dual, $\mathbf{W} = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i$. The instances with $\alpha_i > 0$ are:
options: the support vectors (those on the margin)
items.explain: Only the support vectors (on the margin boundary) have non-zero multipliers; they alone determine $\mathbf{W}$. (Alpaydin §10.9.1.)

items.q: In Alpaydin's **soft-margin** hyperplane, slack variables $\xi_i$ are introduced and the objective adds the term:
items.explain: Soft margin minimizes $\tfrac12\|W\|^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i$; large $C$ penalizes violations more (→ hard margin), small $C$ widens the margin. (Alpaydin §10.9.2.)

items.q: The **kernel trick** lets SVM operate in a high-dimensional space efficiently because the dual depends on data only through:
options: inner (dot) products, which a kernel $K(x_i,x_j)$ computes directly
items.explain: Since training points appear only as dot products, replacing them with $K(x_i,x_j)$ computes the high-dimensional inner product **without the explicit mapping**. (Alpaydin §13, Burges tutorial.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 15.1: if $L$ **independent** base learners are each correct with probability $p > \tfrac12$, the probability a majority vote is correct, as $L$ grows, tends to:
items.explain: This is Condorcet's Jury Theorem: a majority of many independent better-than-random voters is correct with probability $\to 1$ — the statistical basis of ensembles. (Alpaydin §15.2.)

items.q: Alpaydin contrasts bagging and boosting. A key property of **boosting (AdaBoost)** is that base learners are trained:
options: in parallel on equal-weight bootstrap samples
sequentially, each focusing on instances the previous ones misclassified
items.explain: Boosting is sequential: each learner is trained on a reweighted distribution emphasizing previously misclassified instances. Bagging, by contrast, is parallel with equal weights. (Alpaydin §15.5.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 15.2 asks the effect of using L-fold cross-validation instead of bootstrap to make bagging's training sets. Compared to bootstrap, CV folds are:
options: disjoint subsets (sampling without replacement), so they share no instances
always larger than the original set
items.explain: Bootstrap samples *with replacement* (~63% unique, duplicates allowed); CV partitions into *disjoint* folds without replacement — changing the diversity/overlap of the training sets. (Alpaydin, Exercise 15.2.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 4.4 contrasts **incremental (stochastic)** vs **batch** gradient descent. The incremental version:
options: updates weights only after summing errors over all examples
updates weights after each example, approximating true gradient descent with noisier steps
items.explain: Incremental/stochastic GD updates per example — a noisy approximation of the true (batch) gradient that often converges faster and can escape local minima. (Mitchell §4.4.3, Exercise 4.4.)
